sections.heading: Thanking you for grace I did not earn
sections.text: Father, you are endlessly generous. Thank you for the grace you keep showing me, even though I have never deserved it. Thank you for the quiet help of your Spirit, for the times you help me pray when I hardly know how, for the joy that sometimes comes in serving you, and for the hope of finally being with you in heaven. Thank you for sending what I need when I need it, and for bringing life back into me when I feel spiritually flat, cold, and almost dead.
theological_themes: God gives grace freely and continually to the undeserving.
The Holy Spirit helps believers in prayer and spiritual weakness.
Christian service, daily provision, hope of heaven, and spiritual renewal are gifts from God, not achievements.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the Spirit helping believers precisely in their weakness, especially when they do not know how to pray. This grounds the prayer’s gratitude for God’s assistance in prayer.
This passage speaks of God making the spiritually dead alive by mercy and grace. It supports the prayer’s confession that renewal comes from God when the heart feels dead.
Paul expresses confidence that God supplies what his people truly need. This fits the prayer’s thanks for God’s timely and necessary provision.

sections.heading: Resting in your favor more than anyone else’s
sections.text: I do not need to build my life on other people’s approval, because your favor is better than anything they can give me. You know what you are doing with my life. So whether I serve you here or somewhere else, in visible ways or hidden ways, through ease or through trials, let me be ready for whatever work and whatever path you choose for me.
theological_themes: God’s approval is more secure and valuable than human approval.
God governs the circumstances of a believer’s life with wisdom.
The right response to God’s providence is surrendered readiness for his will.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts seeking human approval with living as a servant of Christ. This supports the prayer’s refusal to depend on people’s favor as the foundation of life.
Paul teaches that God works in all things for the good of those who belong to him. This gives biblical weight to trusting God’s wisdom in varied places, duties, and trials.
Peter tells suffering believers to entrust themselves to their faithful Creator while continuing to do good. That matches the prayer’s desire to serve calmly under whatever trials God permits.

sections.heading: Admitting how deeply I need you
sections.text: No one needs your grace more than I do. And still, I have treated your grace lightly more often than I want to admit. My heart can be so slow, dull, and half-awake toward you. Please humble me deeply for loving you so little. Every time I believe, repent, obey, pray, or love in any real way, I am in debt to you again, because even that is your help at work in me.
theological_themes: Human sin remains serious even in those who have received grace.
Every act of spiritual life depends on God’s enabling grace.
True humility comes from seeing both personal sin and total dependence on God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul reminds believers that what they have has been received, leaving no room for boasting. This directly supports the prayer’s confession that every grace and every act of grace comes from God.
Peter calls believers to humility under God’s mighty hand. The prayer asks God to humble the heart because pride and spiritual dullness are not self-cured.
David asks God for a clean heart and renewed spirit after sin. This illuminates the prayer’s plea for inner renewal rather than mere outward improvement.

sections.heading: Putting all my hope in your mercy
sections.text: When I look honestly at myself, I have nothing to brag about. Left to myself, I keep drifting away from you. If I ever make it safely home to you, it will be because you wanted to save me and kept me by your grace. So I come to you as I really am: weak, needy, often wounded, and easily overlooked. I throw myself on your endless goodness. I do not expect lasting happiness from anywhere but you.
theological_themes: Salvation is grounded in God’s grace rather than human worthiness or performance.
The believer’s hope rests in God’s will, mercy, and keeping power.
God himself is the only final source of lasting joy and happiness.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a ground for boasting. This supports the prayer’s rejection of self-confidence before God.

Jesus connects the Father’s saving will with the Son keeping and raising those who come to him. This supports the prayer’s confidence that reaching heaven depends on God’s gracious purpose and preservation.
The psalm locates fullness of joy in God’s presence. This grounds the prayer’s claim that no lasting happiness can finally be found apart from God.

sections.heading: Asking to be made ready for what you give me to do
sections.text: Give me the grace I need for the work you are actually calling me to do. Make me steady and willing in every season. Keep me humble, serious about what matters, and free from the grip of sin. Teach me to say yes to your will, not with clenched teeth, but with trust. Shape me so that my life fits what you want.
theological_themes: God equips his people for the particular service he calls them to do.
Sanctification includes humility, steadiness, self-denial, and putting sin to death.
A surrendered life seeks conformity to God’s will rather than control over circumstances.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says God works in believers both to desire and to do what pleases him. This supports the request for God to make the person ready and willing for his work.
Paul calls believers to put sinful patterns to death and live as those being renewed. This clarifies the prayer’s request to be mortified as a desire for holiness, not self-punishment.
Paul urges believers to offer themselves to God and be transformed so they may discern his will. This fits the prayer’s closing desire to be conformed to God’s will.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly emphasizes God’s sovereign grace as the only reason the believer will reach heaven. That monergistic emphasis is doctrinally contested among some Christian traditions, but it is central to the prayer and has been preserved as dependence on God’s mercy and keeping power rather than softened into general optimism.

The word “mortified” in the original means putting sin to death, not becoming emotionally numb, gloomy, or self-hating. The adaptation renders it as freedom from the grip of sin and seriousness about holiness.

The original’s rejection of “the favour of man” could sound like contempt for people or Christian community. It has been rendered as refusing to build life on human approval, while not denying the biblical goodness of loving and receiving help from others.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Condescension” was interpreted as God’s gracious stooping kindness toward an undeserving person, not as patronizing distance.
“Influences and assistances of thy Spirit” was rendered as the Spirit’s quiet help in weakness and prayer, preserving the experiential dependence without using older devotional vocabulary.

“Special grace to fit me for special services” was interpreted as asking God for particular enabling grace for particular callings and duties, not as a request for spiritual superiority or unusual status.
“Calm and resigned” was rendered as steady, willing trust in God’s will, to avoid implying passive fatalism while preserving surrender.
